citation: 'New Things in Town. A Queer House Out on the Avenue. Reaper Man Glessner's Dutch House in the Aristocratic Precincts of Prairie Avenue.' Unidentified Chicago newspaper, undated (late 1887 by the museum's reading), a clipping pasted in the Glessners' scrapbook; transcribed by the Glessner House Museum, 'Queer, Quaint, and . . . Dutch??', The Story of a House (blog), 8 June 2015.
author: unsigned; newspaper not identified
date: late 1887 (the blog's dating; the clipping carries no date or title of paper)
describes_date: 1887, while the house was being finished ('the workmen are just now putting the inner and finishing touches upon' it)
repository: The Glessners' scrapbook, Glessner House (per the blog; not seen). Read only in the blog's transcription.
locator: The article as transcribed in the blog post: the paragraph beginning 'This Dutch house belongs to J. J. Glessner', from 'Given, a long, narrow lot' to 'That is Mr. Glessner's conservatory on the roof.'
rights_note: An 1887 newspaper text would be in the public domain, but the paper and issue are unidentified and only a museum blog's transcription was read; held at check_required and cited in text only.
access_notes: READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, NOT AT THE PAGE. Read 2026-11-07 (T-3488) from the live blog post (HTML 101,498 bytes, sha256 926d33a85463b33f813022b9a69fe825ba1ea8cf79b90ba2dff44cedea2b1dbe). THE NEWSPAPER IS NOT IDENTIFIED: the blog says 'The newspaper in which it was published is not identified, but it appears to date to the latter part of 1887'. The research note for T-3488 calls it the Chicago Herald; nothing read here supports that name, so the record does not carry it. No scan was found.
note: Read (transcription): 'Given, a long, narrow lot – 75 x 160. Wanted – a large, well-lighted house, with stable and yard. ... The stable is really in the rear end of the house, but separated from it by a solid, unbroken wall. The court, 40 x 100, rivals in beauty the best examples to be found in the old world. It is the yard of the mansion, completely shut out from the view of neighbors or passers-by, and is to be sodded and adorned with fountain and flowers and a neat bit of shrubbery. Overlooking the court, at the angle of the house, is a stone porch, and a broad staircase leads from the library and dining-room to the yard. Just back of the Dutch roof is a sort of tower, indistinctly shown in our illustration. That is Mr. Glessner's conservatory on the roof.' What it gives of the court is an INTENTION of late 1887 ('is to be'), not a record of what was planted; the museum's own note on the same post says the fountain and gardens were dropped (glessner_blog_2015_06_queer_quaint_dutch). The figures are a reporter's round numbers.
what_it_supplies: the court as the house's yard, enclosed from the street and the neighbours, about 40 by 100 ft by the reporter's figure
the plan in late 1887 to sod the court and set a fountain, flowers and shrubbery in it (an intention)
a stone porch at the house's angle over the court and a broad stair from the library and dining-room down to it
the stable at the rear, walled off from the house
a conservatory in the tower behind the roof, by the reporter's account
what_it_does_not_supply: the newspaper's name or the issue's date
what was actually planted, in 1887 or in 1904
a reading of the printed page
